entries.german: 1319: Als nach dem im August 1319 erfolgten Tod des kinderlosen Markgrafen Waldemar von Brandenburg, König Johann von Böhmen Ansprüche auf dessen theihveise Besitzungen erhol), erlangte er zwar die Mark Budissin, hinsichtlich Görlitz kam ihm jedoch sein Schwager, Herzog Heinrich von Jaucr und Förstenberg zuvor. Daher zog der König zu Anfang September mit #00 Mann von Prag aus, um seinen Ansprüchen Nachdruck zu verschaffen. Ilm begleiteten in diesen Feldztig persönlich Herzog Nicolaus von Troppau, Peter von Rosenberg, Wilhelm von Landstein, Hynek Berka von Duba, Thimo von Kolditz, die Brüder Friedrieh, Hermann und Fr ice k, al. Fritzko, von Schönburg, Benes von Michelsberg, Ulrich von Zebrak und Fried mann von Smoyno. Die ersten Feindseligkeiten wurden gegen Herzog Heinrich ausgeübt, aber schon am 22. Sept. kam es im Lager bei Oclsnitz zu einem Vergleich, kraft dessen Herzog Heinrich zu Gunsten des Königs entsagte und nur Görlitz und Lauban erblich, Zittau aber pfandweise erhielt. In dieser Urkunde erscheinen obige drei Brüder als Zeugen. Palacky II. 2. 136 ff.. Schotter I, 225. Cod. dipl. Lus. sup. ed. 2. 1 p. 236, Balb. misc. VIII. 268. Beckler How. II. 3, 2, Ludewig rel. Dec. desselben Jahres compromittirt Hermann von Schönburg, schonenburch, in einer Streitsache mit seinem Oheim Borso von Riesenburg auf den Ausspruch der Schiedsmänner Otto von Bergovv, Friedrich dem Aeltesten von Schönburg, Ulmann von Thyfinbach, henrich Drewiz und Albrecht von Lvtitz, die sich zu Pirna versammeln sollen und setzt zum Pfände Haus Honstein. entries.english:
1319: After the childless Margrave Waldemar of Brandenburg died in August 1319, King Johann of Bohemia asserted claims to some of Waldemar’s possessions. He obtained the March of Budissin, but his brother-in-law, Duke Heinrich of Jauer and Fürstenberg, had forestalled him with respect to Görlitz. At the beginning of September, therefore, the king left Prague with [the source is damaged here: “#00”] men to press his claims. He was personally accompanied on this campaign by Duke Nicolaus of Troppau, Peter von Rosenberg, Wilhelm von Landstein, Hynek Berka von Duba, Thimo von Kolditz, the brothers Friedrich, Hermann and Fricek (also called Fritzko) von Schönburg, Benes von Michelsberg, Ulrich von Zebrak and Friedmann von Smoyno. The first hostilities were directed against Duke Heinrich, but on September 22 an agreement was reached in the camp near Oelsnitz. Under it Duke Heinrich renounced his claims in favor of the king, retaining Görlitz and Lauban hereditarily and Zittau as a pledge. The three Schönburg brothers appear as witnesses in the instrument. The editor cites a number of published sources.

On December 28 of that year, Hermann von Schönburg submitted his dispute with his uncle Borso von Riesenburg to the decision of arbiters: Otto von Bergow, Friedrich der Älteste von Schönburg, Ulmann von Thyfinbach, Henrich Drewiz and Albrecht von Lvtitz, who were to meet at Pirna. As security, he pledged Hohnstein Castle. The deed is dated at Girsberg, at the castle, on December 28, 1320.

“We, Hermann von Schönburg, acknowledge in this open letter and make known to all who hear or read it that we have submitted all our matters against our uncle, Lord Borso von Riesenburg—whether concerning debt, surety, damages or any other cause involving money—to the noble lords Otto von Bergow, Friedrich der Älteste von Schönburg, Ulmann von Thyfinbach, Henrich Drewiz and Albrecht von Lvtitz. Whatever they direct us to do, whether by agreement or law, we shall obey without objection. We shall appear at Pirna on the eighth day after the next feast of Our Lady, without fail unless urgent necessity or illness prevents us.

“If we do not do so, then I, Hermann von Schönburg, have pledged my house at Hohnstein, with everything belonging to it that I have acquired and that is due to me, as a pledge according to the law of pledges until I fulfill this obligation. Albrecht von Lvtitz has promised that, should I fail in this matter, he will hold the house for Lord Borso von Riesenburg until I have performed what I promised, and will not diminish our principal property. We further acknowledge that if the five arbiters do not agree, we shall follow the decision of the majority among them and carry it out as though all five had ordered it.

“To ensure that this agreement and promise is kept fully and faithfully, we give him this letter, confirmed with our seal. It was written and issued after the birth of Christ in the year one thousand three hundred and twenty, on the feast of the Holy Innocents, at Girsberg, at the castle.”

The editor identifies the original deed in the Dresden Main State Archive, no. 2185, and notes that the Schönburg seal is missing. For the relationship to Riesenburg, see Reg. 1281.
